A whole characteristic line with smooth forcing

Author: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra. Self-checked by the writing AI; no independent review.

An equation can have a smooth right-hand side while its solution has one persistent singular covector along an entire line. We construct such a solution for a constant-coefficient operator of real principal type. The solution can have any prescribed finite number of continuous derivatives. Its ordinary wavefront is exactly one positive covector ray over the chosen characteristic line.

The ingredients are the actual conic projectors of Boundary regularity and conic decomposition, Lemma 2 and Theorem 4; the signed parametrices and their commutation identity in Analytic parametrices and straight characteristics, Theorem 3 and Lemma 4; and the ordinary convolution bound in Keeping zero covectors in kernel operations, Corollary 7. The functional foundation, Sections 6, 14.1–14.2 and 19, proves the complete-metric Baire theorem and the countable-seminorm metric. The Fourier foundation, F1–F5, supplies inversion and compact-test Fourier estimates. We give the completeness and wave-packet arguments needed for the particular function space here.

6. Exact realization on the whole line

Theorem 6 (one global characteristic ray). For every integer , every operator satisfying (1)–(2), every nonzero characteristic , and every , there is a complex function such that and For , the function can be chosen not on any neighborhood of zero.

Proof. First take . If every were near zero, Lemma 4 would give a finite estimate (17). Choose the packets of Lemma 5 for exactly its finitely many seminorms. Its right-hand side is , whereas (23), with , has absolute value at least for large . This is impossible. Hence some is not on any neighborhood of zero.

Such a function is not smooth near zero. Lemma 1 supplies a wavefront covector over zero, and (6) forces it to be a positive multiple of . Positive conicity then gives . Its forcing is smooth on all of , so Lemma 2 propagates that covector over the whole line . Positive scaling gives every pair on the right of (29). The reverse inclusion follows from the defining smoothness off and (6). Translating this function by proves the general case: constant-coefficient differentiation commutes with translation, and translating a cutoff Fourier witness multiplies its transform by a phase of absolute value one. Thus wavefront base points translate exactly.

The theorem prescribes ordinary smooth wavefront. It does not assert that the analytic wavefront is the same set. It gives smooth forcing, without requiring that forcing to be zero. Both distinctions matter: finite differentiability allows ordinary singularities, and a separate solvability argument would be needed to subtract a smooth solution with that forcing.

Exercise 1 (foundation: a real solution cannot select just one sign). Show that a real distribution cannot have exactly the nonempty wavefront in (29).

Solution. For a compact distribution , , by the Fourier pairing and complex conjugation. Conjugating a cutoff witness gives a witness in the opposite cone, and conjugating twice proves For real , its wavefront is symmetric under . The nonempty positive ray in (29) is not symmetric. Exercise 4 (advanced: why the full line is necessary). Under the hypotheses of Theorem 6, can smooth forcing coexist with a wavefront consisting exactly of a nonempty finite closed segment of the line in (29), with the same positive covector ray?

Solution. No. Select any point of that segment and the covector . Since the forcing is smooth globally, Lemma 2 puts the same covector over every point of the entire line, contradicting the asserted finite segment. A finite-ray construction with singular forcing at its endpoints has different hypotheses; those endpoints prevent applying (7) across the boundary of the segment. Smooth global forcing is the precise reason the current result prescribes the whole line.

Exercise 5 (intermediate: the finite neighborhood is used in two different ways). Explain why the radius of and the truncation length are chosen after the finite seminorm list in Lemma 4. Show that neither parameter needs to depend on .

Solution. Finitely many off-line seminorms involve finitely many positive distances . A fixed smaller than half their minimum makes every one vanish. Finitely many forcing seminorms involve a largest derivative order . A fixed makes (25) at most for all of them. Once these choices are made, all amplitudes are fixed, so their compact derivative and Fourier constants are independent of . Infinitely many off-line seminorms would have distances tending to zero, and infinitely many forcing seminorms would have no largest order. The Baire conclusion supplies exactly the finiteness that makes both choices possible.

Exercise 6 (advanced: no automatic homogeneous correction). Suppose a separately proved theorem supplies a smooth global solution of for the function in Theorem 6. What conclusion follows, and which step is conditional?

Solution. Then satisfies . A smooth summand has empty wavefront, so the finite-sum rule gives ; applying it to gives the reverse inclusion. Hence has exactly (29). If were near zero in the untranslated case, so would , contradicting the choice in Theorem 6. The existence of such a global smooth is the conditional step. It does not follow from the mere smoothness of the right-hand side or from the present Baire argument.

Solution. The gradient is , and . The base line is , . Its spatial speed relative to time is one, in the fixed direction . Over every point the covectors are positive multiples of ; these retain one time-covector sign even though the base parameter runs in both directions. Applying Theorem 6 to the opposite characteristic covector is a separate valid choice. One need not conjugate an equation with complex lower coefficients to obtain it.

Proof locations and mathematical source

  • Boundary regularity and conic decomposition, Lemma 2 and Theorem 4, gives the exact smooth localization estimate and direction projectors. Analytic parametrices and straight characteristics, Theorem 3 and Lemma 4, and Keeping zero covectors in kernel operations, Corollary 7, supply the signed inverse and convolution steps used in Lemma 2.
  • The functional foundation, Sections 6, 14.1–14.2 and 19, supplies complete-metric Baire and its selected logical basis. Lemma 3 verifies completeness for the actual space used here; Lemma 4 derives its estimate directly.
  • Lars Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I, second edition, 2003 reprint, Theorem 8.3.8 and its proof, pp. 278–280, is the mathematical antecedent for global singular-ray realization.
